steps.justification: If a prime p divides 1, then there exists an integer c with 1 = pc. But p ≥ 2 (definition of prime), so for any integer c: if c ≤ 0 then pc ≤ 0 < 1, and if c ≥ 1 then pc ≥ p ≥ 2 > 1. So no integer c satisfies 1 = pc, contradicting p | 1. Therefore no prime divides 1.

verdicts.reason: The cited rule exists and is applied correctly. Proof by contradiction is a standard classical proof method: to prove P, temporarily assume ¬P and derive a contradiction; see Stanford CS103 and TU Delft notes: https://stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs103/cs103.1266/guide_to_proofs and https://interactivetextbooks.tudelft.nl/delftse-foundations-of-computation/content/logic/proof-by-contradiction.html. The assumed statement, “There are only finitely many prime numbers,” is the negation of “There are infinitely many primes,” under the standard set-theoretic meaning that an infinite set is one that is not finite; see MathWorld: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Finite.html. The step only opens a temporary contradiction assumption and preserves the original goal, so it introduces no hidden mathematical premise beyond the cited classical proof rule.

[PEDANTRY OVERRIDE] The only issue is a harmless notational shortening of the assumption label from `Assumption H (for contradiction)` to `Assumption H`. The underlying assumption is unchanged, and the proof context remains clear from State 1 and later use of contradiction. The cited definition correctly supports adding `2 is a prime number`, so the rejection demands formatting rigor rather than identifying a real proof error.

The cited principle is real and correctly applied. Sources define an enumeration of a finite set as a bijection from {1,...,n} to the set, and define finite sets by the existence of such a bijection/listing (ProofWiki: https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Definition:Enumeration, MathWorld: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FiniteSet.html). Under Assumption H, the primes form a finite collection; since the previous state has `2 is a prime number`, that collection is nonempty, so its cardinality is some `n >= 1`. Therefore it is legitimate to introduce symbols `p_1, ..., p_n` as a complete enumeration of all primes. The step does not introduce an extra mathematical premise beyond unpacking finiteness, nonemptiness, and enumeration notation.

The step is justified. Published references define a prime as a positive integer/integer greater than 1 with only the divisors 1 and itself; for integers, greater than 1 implies at least 2. Sources: Wolfram MathWorld (https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PrimeNumber.html) and Britannica (https://www.britannica.com/science/prime-number). From the previous state, “complete enumeration of all primes” means each listed p_i is prime, so universal instantiation gives: for every i in {1,...,n}, p_i is prime, hence p_i >= 2. No hidden premise is needed, and the added line is the only change.

The step is valid. From the previous state, p_1, ..., p_n is a finite list with n >= 1, and each p_i is prime, hence an integer. Therefore the finite product p_1 · p_2 · ... · p_n is an integer, and adding 1 gives an integer. Introducing a fresh symbol N by the definition N := (p_1 · p_2 · ... · p_n) + 1 uses no hidden premise and excludes no valid edge case.

The computation is correct. The previous state explicitly gives n >= 1 and, for every listed factor, p_i >= 2. Thus the product has at least one factor and all factors are at least 2, so p_1...p_n >= 2, including the edge case n = 1. From the definition N = p_1...p_n + 1, it follows that N >= 3 > 1. No hidden premise or excluded valid edge case is needed.

The cited result exists and matches standard elementary number theory. For example, UMD lecture notes state: “Every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor” and prove it by well-ordering (https://www.math.umd.edu/~immortal/MATH406/lecturenotes/ch3-1.pdf, lines 8-14). LibreTexts also states the same lemma and gives the same well-ordering argument (https://math.libretexts.org/.../2.01%3A_The_Sieve_of_Eratosthenes, lines 223-225). The step does not yet apply the theorem to N; it only adds this valid universal theorem to the proof state. The only change from BEFORE to AFTER is that added theorem, and the citation justifies it. No hidden premise is needed at this step.

The step is justified. The exact rule is more precisely universal instantiation plus modus ponens, or universal modus ponens: a universal conditional can be applied to a particular domain element satisfying its antecedent. Verified source: https://www.csm.ornl.gov/~sheldon/ds/sec1.8.html. The number-theory premise also exists as a standard lemma: every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor. Verified source: https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Combinatorics_and_Discrete_Mathematics/Elementary_Number_Theory_%28Raji%29/02%3A_Prime_Numbers/2.01%3A_The_Sieve_of_Eratosthenes. In the previous state, N > 1 is explicit, and N is an integer from its definition as a finite product of primes plus 1. Instantiating the universal statement at N yields exactly: there exists a prime q such that q divides N. No extra state changes or hidden premises are introduced.

The cited divisibility fact is real and correctly applied. Standard integer divisibility says a | b iff b = ka for some integer k; see LibreTexts: https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Combinatorics_and_Discrete_Mathematics/Elementary_Number_Theory_%28Raji%29/01%3A_Introduction/1.03%3A_Divisibility_and_the_Division_Algorithm. For any fixed i, p_i is one factor in p_1 · ... · p_n, so the product equals p_i times the product of the remaining integer factors. In the n = 1 case this is just p_1 = p_1 · 1, so no edge case breaks the argument. Therefore p_i divides p_1 · ... · p_n for each i, and the citation justifies exactly the single added statement without smuggling in an extra premise.

The cited result exists and is standard. For example, LibreTexts states that if an integer divides two integers, then it divides any integer linear combination of them; taking coefficients 1 and -1 gives d | (a - b). A Kansas State number theory text states the difference property directly: if d|a and d|b, then d|(a-b). Sources: https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Combinatorics_and_Discrete_Mathematics/Elementary_Number_Theory_%28Raji%29/01%3A_Introduction/1.03%3A_Divisibility_and_the_Division_Algorithm and https://math.ksu.edu/~cochrane/m706/m706s20/m706s20notes.pdf. The proof given in the citation is correct: from a=dk and b=dl with k,l integers, a-b=d(k-l), and k-l is an integer. In this step the property is only introduced for later use, not yet applied to p_i or N. It justifies the sole change from BEFORE to AFTER, namely adding the divisibility property. No hidden premise is used here beyond the standard meaning of divisibility over integers; if one uses a convention requiring the divisor to be nonzero, that condition is implicit in the notation d|a and is satisfied in the later intended use because d will be a prime p_i.

The computation is correct. For any fixed i in {1,...,n}, the prior state gives p_i | (p_1...p_n). Under the conditional assumption p_i | N, the stated divisibility property yields p_i | (N - p_1...p_n). Since N was defined as (p_1...p_n)+1, the difference is 1, so p_i | 1. No extra bound or edge-case assumption is being introduced; n >= 1 and the relevant divisibility facts are already available.

The added claim is justified. The cited argument uses the standard definition that a prime is a positive integer greater than 1, hence at least 2, matching MathWorld's definition: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PrimeNumber.html. It also uses the standard divisibility definition that d divides n when n/d is an integer, equivalently n = dc for some integer c: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Divides.html. The case split on integer c is supported by the trichotomy/total-order property: https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Trichotomy_Law_(Ordering). Applied to 1, if p is prime and p | 1, then 1 = pc for some integer c; c <= 0 gives pc <= 0, while c >= 1 gives pc >= p >= 2, so no integer c works. This establishes exactly the new state item, 'No prime number divides 1', and introduces no unsupported extra conclusion.

The cited rule exists and has the stated form: from P -> Q and not Q, infer not P; see Britannica: https://www.britannica.com/topic/modus-ponens. It is applied correctly here. For arbitrary i in {1,...,n}, step 11 gives p_i | N -> p_i | 1. Since p_i is already known to be prime, step 12 gives not(p_i | 1). Modus tollens gives not(p_i | N), and universal generalization yields the added statement for every i. This is the only change from BEFORE to AFTER, and it uses no hidden premise.

The step is justified. The needed underlying rules are real: existential instantiation permits treating the fresh q from step 8 as a witness with q | N (see https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Existential_Instantiation), equality elimination/substitution permits replacing q by p_i if q = p_i (see Stanford Logic: https://logic.stanford.edu/intrologic/extras/equality.html), and contradiction plus quantifier negation supports concluding there is no i with q = p_i, i.e. q ≠ p_i for all i (see https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Proof_by_Contradiction and https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Mathematical_Logic_and_Proof/Proofs_and_Concepts_-_The_Fundamentals_of_Abstract_Mathematics_(Morris_and_Morris)/04%3A_First-Order_Logic/4.03%3A_Negations). Applied here: for any listed i, if q = p_i, then from q | N we get p_i | N, contradicting step 13. No extra number-theory premise is smuggled in, and the only new assertion in AFTER is accounted for.

The step is justified. The cited conventions are real: an enumeration lists a set so that every element appears, and a contradiction is a statement of the form P and not-P. Sources checked: https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Philosophy/Sets_Logic_Computation_%28Zach%29/01%3A_I-_Sets_Relations_Functions/1.04%3A_The_Size_of_Sets/1.4.02%3A_Enumerations_and_Countable_Sets and https://homepage.iis.sinica.edu.tw/~bywang/courses/comp-logic/chapter-1-1.pdf. Here, step 8 gives q is prime, step 3 says every prime is among p_1,...,p_n, so q = p_i for some i. Step 14 says q ≠ p_i for every i. Those are incompatible, so adding “Contradiction” is correct. This assumes the proof’s already-used convention that q is the fixed witness from step 8.

The cited rule exists and is correctly applied. Proof by contradiction/reductio is a standard classical inference rule: sources state that to prove X, assume X is false, derive a contradiction, then conclude X is true; ProofWiki also gives the form that if an assumption φ yields contradiction, infer ¬φ (https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Proof_by_Contradiction; https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs103/cs103.1266/guide_to_proofs). Here Assumption H was explicitly introduced for contradiction and State 15 contains a contradiction derived under H, so H may be discharged. The remaining conversion from “not only finitely many primes” to “there are infinitely many primes” is also justified by the standard definition/dichotomy: a set that is not finite is infinite (MathWorld: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Finite.html). No extra premise is smuggled in beyond standard classical logic and the standard meaning of “infinitely many.”
